analysis.one_liner: Locks in existing federal fuel economy and tailpipe emissions standards for cars through model year 2025.
analysis.headline: The bill never left committee: introduced in February 2019 with 74 cosponsors, it was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and never received a markup or a floor vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: In 2012, the government set rules requiring new cars and light trucks to get steadily more fuel-efficient and emit less pollution through model year 2025, targeting a fleet average of about 46.3 miles per gallon. In 2019, the administration was working to weaken those rules, so Rep. Doris Matsui introduced this bill to write the standards into law and bar regulators from making them any looser. The bill was sent to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and never moved again.
analysis.who_benefits: Drivers, who would save money at the gas pump as vehicles meet roughly 46.3 mpg fleet-wide by 2025; everyone exposed to vehicle pollution, since the standards were projected to cut 540 million metric tons of greenhouse gases and 1.2 billion barrels of oil use over the vehicles' lifetimes; and state air regulators whose single national program would be preserved.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Drivers and people breathing vehicle pollution

how_it_helps.text: The bill requires regulators to keep fuel economy and greenhouse gas standards at least as stringent as the 2012 rules through model year 2025, protecting consumers' fuel savings from being rolled back.

The standards it preserves were projected to reach a fleet-wide average of 46.3 miles per gallon by 2025, cutting 540 million metric tons of greenhouse gases and 1.2 billion barrels of oil consumption over the life of the vehicles.
It bars agencies from creating new compliance loopholes, including by changing how credits for fuel economy are traded or created.

analysis.who_pays: Automakers, which would face the full compliance costs of the stricter standards rather than the looser ones the industry was seeking in 2019, and the oil industry, which would lose gasoline demand as new cars burn less fuel. Car buyers could see some of the compliance cost passed into sticker prices.

drawbacks.text: The bill strips regulators of flexibility: it forbids any action that could effectively reduce the stringency of the standards through 2025, so if compliance turned out to cost more than projected, agencies could not ease them without another act of Congress.
Stricter fuel economy rules add engineering costs that automakers can pass into new-vehicle prices, and critics argue that pushes some buyers to keep older, dirtier cars longer.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill is a defensive measure: it preserves standards that a 2017 government review found feasible for the industry, with multiple compliance pathways, and that were projected to save drivers fuel money far exceeding vehicle cost increases. The main cost is compliance expense for automakers and higher upfront vehicle prices; the tradeoff is real but small next to the projected fuel savings and emissions cuts.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Rep. Doris Matsui introduced the Clean and Efficient Cars Act of 2019 on February 5, 2019, with 19 original cosponsors.
The bill would convert the 2012 EPA and NHTSA fuel economy and greenhouse gas rules for vehicles through model year 2025 into statutory requirements and bar any action that reduces their stringency.
Seventy-four House Democrats cosponsored the bill; no Republican did.

The bill was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee on the day of introduction, and the action record shows no further activity — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote — through the end of the 116th Congress.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died, automakers seeking looser standards and oil producers kept the fuel economy rules open to rollback through ordinary rulemaking rather than locked in by statute.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Automakers wanting looser rules and oil producers

sides.party_line_note: Every cosponsor was a Democrat — 74 of 231 House Democrats — and no Republican supported the bill; it never reached a vote, so no roll-call record exists.

industries.note: The bill would deny automakers the looser standards they were seeking in 2019 and hold them to the 2012 rules' compliance costs, which can feed into vehicle prices. But those same rules were negotiated with automakers and found feasible in a 2017 government review, and they save drivers fuel money.

Higher fuel economy reduces gasoline demand — the standards the bill locks in were projected to cut oil use by 1.2 billion barrels over the vehicles' lifetimes — so the industry benefits from any weakening of the rules.
